title: Capacity Rehearsal & Decision Playbook: SLO-Driven Load Drills
author: Aisha Khatri
body:
Overview
This playbook describes a repeatable, SLO-focused capacity rehearsal process for Redwood Inference services. The goal is to validate decision-making under pressure: determine when to scale, throttle, or failover to fallbacks while preserving customer SLAs and minimizing error budget consumption. This document covers planning, execution, telemetry collection, operator decision flows, automated scripts, and post-drill analysis.

Why we run capacity rehearsals
- Validate capacity planning assumptions against real workload shapes (burstiness, prefix reuse, KV cache hit patterns).
- Exercise autoscaling and emergency procedures so runbooks work under time pressure.
- Measure how error budgets are consumed and calibrate SLO thresholds and routing policies.
- Improve confidence in graceful degradation behavior and fallback routing.

Scope and applicability
- Applies to public customer-facing inference routes, critical internal control-plane services (scheduler, autoscaler), and the routing layer.
- Not intended for isolated developer environments — drills should run in canary / preprod and staged production windows as described below.

Key roles and responsibilities
- Drill Captain: owns scheduling, communications, and go/no-go (default: oncall SRE Lead).
- Telemetry Lead: ensures dashboards & traces are ready, runs PromQL queries during the drill.
- Runbook Operator(s): execute scale/throttle/fallback steps and observe effects.
- Incident Communicator: posts status updates on #sre-drills and updates the drill timeline doc.
- Engineering SME(s): model-serving and routing owners (participate during escalation).

SLOs and success criteria
- Primary SLOs observed: 99th percentile inference latency (p99 <= 750ms for hosted-api-standard), error rate (5xx) < 0.5% per-minute window, availability 99.95% weekly.
- Drill success: operator decisions executed within target times and no unplanned customer-visible outages for more than the allowed error budget slice (<= 0.01% of total weekly budget).
- Failure conditions: >2x expected error-budget consumption rate, inability to scale/fallback within configured timeout, or missing telemetry feeds.

Pre-drill checklist (must be green before start)
1) Schedule and approvals
   - Drill Captain confirms window and stakeholder sign-off (email + #sre-drills ack).
   - Business hours vs nighttime drills identified; high-risk customers notified when applicable.
2) Environment verification
   - Target environment (canary/prod-staged/limited-prod) selected with explicit percentage of live traffic.
   - Autoscaler and routing control-plane healthy (health-checks green for 1h).
3) Telemetry and observability
   - Dashboards pinned: SLO overview, request-rate by route, KV cache hit-ratio, GPU utilization, queue-depth, model latency histograms.
   - Trace sampling enabled for affected routes, and OpenTelemetry collector endpoints validated.
   - Alerting mute plan applied for expected noise and documented in timeline.
4) Safety gates and throttles
   - Preconfigured emergency throttle rules exist and tested in staging.
   - Canary fallback model variants available and validated.
5) Communication plan
   - Slack channels, Zoom bridge, status page contact list, and incident templated messages ready.

Drill types (choose one per rehearsal)
- Gradual Load Ramp: synthetic traffic increased by 10% every 5 minutes until target or error budget triggers; used to validate autoscaler and burst handling.
- Sudden Surge: a short, high-intensity spike (2-5x baseline) to validate backpressure and graceful degradation.
- Component Failure Simulation: intentionally stop a serving pool or region to validate failover & routing policies.
- Cache Poisoning / Cold-KV Run: clear prefix caches to simulate cache warmup behavior and memory pressure.

Execution procedure (step-by-step)
1) Pre-start (T-30m): final go/no-go check; confirm mute rules; Telemetry Lead opens the drill dashboard.
2) Start (T0): announce start with baseline metrics snapshot.
3) Apply load per chosen drill type using load-generator harness (see Automation snippets).
4) Monitor live metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, queue depth, GPU queue length, autoscaler scale events, and error budget burn rate. Use the following PromQL examples:
   - Request rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{route=~"/api/.*"}[1m])) by (route)
   - p99 latency (histogram): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
   - Error budget burn (1m): increase(errors_total[1m]) / increase(requests_total[1m])
5) Decision checkpoints (every 5 minutes)
   - If p99 > 750ms OR 5xx > 0.5%: Telemetry Lead recommends mitigation path.
   - Operator evaluates Decision Tree (below) and executes Scale/Throttle/Fallback.
6) End (T+drill_duration): stop load generator, capture final snapshots, and begin structured post-drill analysis.

Decision tree: scale vs throttle vs failover
- Node A: Is autoscaler able to add capacity within 3 minutes?
   - Yes -> Scale up (see Scale play).
   - No -> Node B.
- Node B: Is there a compatible fallback model or lower-capacity variant available with acceptable quality?
   - Yes -> Route 20% of traffic to fallback variant, monitor error budget for 10 minutes; if stable, increase routing to 50%.
   - No -> Node C.
- Node C: Apply graded throttling: 1) soft-rate-limit by user tier (reduce non-paid or best-effort routes), 2) reject noisy prefixes, 3) emergency global reject with explicit customer communications.

Scale play (operators)
1) Kick autoscaler manually: kubectl -n serving scale deployment/model-serving --replicas=N (target N computed from capacity table).
2) If using dedicated pools, trigger pool-burst request via infra CLI: infractl capacity request --pool serving-dedicated --gpus 8 --ttl 30m
3) Verify new instances register with routing layer and begin accepting traffic.
4) Observe latency tail and error rate for 2 consecutive evaluation windows (2x 1m).

Throttle play (operators)
1) Apply rate-limit config for affected route: redwoodctl routes update --route /api/generate --rate-limit 50rps --burst 20
2) If prefix-based, apply dynamic prefix throttle: redwoodctl traffic throttle --prefix noisy-prefix --limit 10rps
3) Communicate to customers via status page and in-app banners (templated messages in "Communication templates").

Failover/fallback play
1) Update routing policy to direct a percentage of traffic to fallback model version:
   redwoodctl routing update --route /api/generate --fallback-model rdm-v2-quant --weight 20
2) Monitor model quality metrics (reranking accuracy, sampling divergence) and customer feedback.

Post-drill analysis and reporting
- Required artifacts: raw telemetry timeline (CSV/JSON), decision timeline, runbook actions executed, command logs, and operator notes.
- Post-drill report template (use in retrospective):
   - Drill objective: (short)
   - Drill type and environment: (e.g., sudden surge — canary-prod 5%)
   - Timeline of events: timestamps and actions taken
   - Key metrics: request-rate, p99, 5xx, CPU/GPU utilization, cache-hit ratio
   - Decision justification: why chosen path (scale/throttle/fallback)
   - What worked: list
   - What failed or was surprising: list
   - Action items (owner + due date): list
- Post-drill retrospective (within 7 days): run a 60-minute blameless session, publish notes to the postmortem board and link to the original runbook.

Instrumentation & automation snippets
- Load generator (k6 example):
  import http from 'k6/http'
  export default function () {
    http.post('https://api.redwood.test/api/generate', JSON.stringify({prompt: 'Test load'}), {headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}})
  }
- Autoscaler manual scale (kubectl):
  kubectl -n serving scale deployment/model-serving --replicas=12
- Sample PromQL to detect autoscaler lag:
  sum(kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable{deployment=~"model-serving.*"}) by (deployment)
- Telemetry collection (CLI):
  redwood-metrics dump --from "2026-02-03T10:00:00Z" --to "2026-02-03T10:20:00Z" --routes "/api/generate" --output drill-telemetry.json

Safety, compliance and customer impact considerations
- Never run full-production-wide sudden surge drills without executive approval and customer notification.
- For regulated customers or private deployments, mirror-only drills should be used (no write-effects).
- Ensure data residency and logging compliance when sharing telemetry externally.

Periodic cadence and continuous improvement
- Recommended cadence: quarterly full-scale rehearsals for critical routes; monthly lightweight smoke drills for autoscaler and routing sanity checks.
- After each drill, update the runbook artifacts and SLO thresholds if evidence indicates a calibration mismatch.
- Maintain a playbook backlog and prioritize automation items that shorten decision time under pressure.

Appendices
A. Capacity reference table (example):
- 1 GPU (A100) can support ~180 requests/sec for model rdm-encoder-small at average token length 64 and KV cache warm.
- 4 GPUs support ~680 requests/sec for rdm-encoder-large under similar conditions.
B. Communications templates: slack / status page / in-app banner (copy-paste ready).
C. Drill run log sample: structured CSV columns: timestamp, metric_snapshot, action, actor, notes.

Related documents and links
- See predictive-slo-driven-capacity-playbook for capacity forecasting assumptions.
- Use the SRE runbook library for escalation and incident-review templates.
